claims.text: The nanoparticles are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid solutions supported on graphene before service exposure.
Laser-induced solid-phase synthesis on graphene enhances nanoparticle structural stability under high-temperature service conditions.
Laser-induced solid-phase synthesis on graphene enhances nanoparticle chemical stability under high-temperature service conditions.
Rapid laser processing creates a defect-engineered nanoparticle–graphene interface.
Laser-generated interfacial defects enhance bonding between the nanoparticles and graphene.
Enhanced nanoparticle–graphene interfacial bonding restricts atomic mobility within the nanoparticles.
Restricted atomic mobility reduces elemental segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Restricted atomic mobility reduces phase demixing during high-temperature exposure.
Laser-synthesized nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than conventionally synthesized nanoparticles.
Laser-synthesized nanoparticles will retain more stable phase compositions than conventionally synthesized nanoparticles.
Laser-synthesized nanoparticles will undergo less morphological change than conventionally synthesized nanoparticles.
The proposed stability effect applies during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The proposed stability effect applies during thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K.
The hypothesis is limited to near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles produced on graphene under the defined laser synthesis conditions.
The validity of the mechanism for other compositions, substrates, and synthesis parameters is untested.
